## Verdict: body is unbalanced

A typical NeurIPS body sits roughly at **Intro 15–20% / Related Work 10–15% / Method 25–30% / Experiments 30–40% / Conclusion <5%**. Yours:

- **Related Work eats half the body (50%, ~1150 words).** That is roughly 3× the conventional share. The four mini-paragraphs (TSFM Adaptation, MoE in FMs, MoE Collapse and Rescue, Normalization in TS) read more like a survey than a positioning section.
- **Method is starved (7%, 164 words of prose).** Figures/equations carry the load, but the actual textual description of RR-MoA is thinner than the contributions list in the intro.
- **Experiments is also light (15%, 353 words).** Tables carry the evidence — but the prose-to-table ratio means a reviewer skimming text gets very little signal between tables.
- **Intro is on the upper edge (23%)** but defensible because it has to pre-load the diagnosis.
- **Conclusion is appropriately tight.**

## What this implies for the spillover work we just did

We compressed prose in Intro, Method, and Results to pull body onto page 9. That was the right move for the page-limit constraint, but it pushed Method/Experiments even thinner relative to Related Work. The structural issue is **Related Work**, not the sections we already trimmed.

## Recommendation (no action taken yet)

If you want a more balanced body, the high-leverage edit is to compress Related Work by 30–40% — fold the *TSFM Adaptation* and *MoE in Foundation Models* paragraphs into shorter "we cite group X for Y; closest precedent is Z because W" sentences, keeping every `\citep` key but cutting the descriptive clauses about each cited work. That recovers ~400 words and lets you give Method or Experiments more breathing room without extending the page count. Want me to draft that compression?

Appendix distribution is fine — §P being the largest is justified because the DLinear-gap-closing argument is the most reviewer-targeted claim and contains the 107/123 evidence headline.
